title: Spread of Indian religions and culture in Southeast Asia
summary: Southeast Asian societies adapted Indian ideas for over a millennium. Funan, active from the first century CE in what is now Cambodia and Vietnam, adopted Indian influences, with Hinduism and Buddhism both prevalent. Sambor Prei Kuk, the Chenla capital of the late 6th and early 7th centuries, blended Indian ideas with animist and Buddhist elements in a style that later led to Khmer art.

uncertainty.note: Indian cultural contact began in the early centuries CE (EBSCO notes Funan active from the first century CE); the classical era of Indianized mainland empires culminated with Angkor, which fell in 1431 CE according to World History Encyclopedia.

as_recorded.value: active from the first century CE

where.modern_name: Sambor Prei Kuk, Kampong Thom Province, Cambodia (anchor for early Hindu-Buddhist statecraft in Chenla and the Khmer realm; process spans Southeast Asia)
where.historical_name: Ishanapura, capital of Chenla; regional kingdoms across mainland and maritime Southeast Asia

importance.justification: Indian religions and art shaped kingdoms across mainland Southeast Asia for over a millennium.

sources.title: Temple Zone of Sambor Prei Kuk, Archaeological Site of Ancient Ishanapura

reviewer_note: Local peoples chose and changed these ideas, so this was not simple transfer. The record ends with the Khmer Empire in 1431, though the influence continued. The pin marks Sambor Prei Kuk.
